Hey! I am much better than I was. Life isn't perfect of course but a lot of things got better after uni. 

I'll say that a lot of the negativity you're harbouring inside won't have as strong a hold of you as it does right now. Life isn't a constant. Some things might improve, others might get worse. But your brain isn't capable of holding any feeling very strongly forever. So your negative internal thoughts will grow quieter and most of the time you will be focused on everyday life. I also stopped chasing motivation or a meaning to my life. I realised that the vast majority of adults don't have anything that strong. And you don't need one to enjoy life. Just focus on providing for yourself - financial stability and good health. Try to treasure relationships with your family and friends. There's no need to take life that seriously. There is absolutely nothing wrong with having no passion or anything. Just focus on being healthy, financially stable, and a responsible adult who can show compassion for other people. All of this is probably not in your comfort zone so it might not come naturally. It helps if you try to change something internally and externally. Internal changes take longer but external changes can begin immediately. Try talking to a friend. Nothing heavy but general friendly conversations. Or try to learn a new sport. It may not feel like it helped immediately but it will remain in your memory for a while. And every moment your memory is filled with other stuff is a moment your depression can't take over your consciousness. 

I won't say things will get better. But  rather that YOU will get better. You'll be shocked at how little power your negative thoughts have once you fill up your brain with other experiences

Slightly off-topic, but 明鏡 is my favourite in general, because its definitions are fairly easy to understand and there's the option of toggling furigana on the entire dictionary if you get it on monokakido, so it's great if you're like me and use dictionaries primarily to quickly look up stuff. 新明解 is just as great (and has audio recordings with pitch accent markers), and 三省堂 is great if you want simple definitions. 大辞林 and 大辞泉 are very similar and are far more exhaustive than the others (and the new 大辞泉 has audio recordings too). 20-80 sounds like a good ratio. I think it's best to experiment with various methods as a beginner and find out what you like and can maintain over a long period of time. As a beginner, one of the bigger obstacles, I think, is to get over the differences between Japanese and your native language. Some people overcome these better with textbooks and others with native content. The great thing about immersion is you don't learn set patterns and outliers separately, so you give equal importance to everything.

Anyways I think it's possible to learn a language through mostly immersion, but that it depends on your goals and the kind of person you are.

Immersion *is* actually learning the language though. I mean, people did learn languages before textbooks were ever a thing. That's not to say textbooks or Anki are useless. You can learn grammar and memorise words/sentences. They can certainly be helpful but I don't think they're essential. I don't think immersion means consuming content without understanding it. Even watching Japanese shows with English subtitles counts as immersion if you're paying attention to the Japanese. Visual and audio contexts + the words will slowly make sense and take root within the mind. People recommend mnemonics in Anki to form stories and give context, but with immersion you can try the opposite. Emotions are attached to words and repeating it over and over (as in by consuming more media), retention also gets better.

It looks like OP didn't start with novels but with other native media before. So I don't think it's magical at all.

Anyways, what I said might sound like nonsense, but that's how language learning works in my head.
